question: Lube oil sump levels were low and in heavy seas the generators lost lube oil suction, tripped on low lube oil pressure and the ship blacked out and lost propulsion near a lee shore.
A containership lost electrical power twice while departing port, lost propulsion and steering, and struck a bridge.
An online generator's automatic voltage regulator malfunctioned earlier and was never properly repaired; later the ship lost electrical power and propulsion while manoeuvring to the dock.
Main engine automatically shut down after a false oil mist detector alarm caused by water vapour after replacing a cylinder head gasket in humid conditions, and the ship collided with another vessel.
Debris like O-ring material in the steering gear hydraulic oil seized a control motor and the rudder locked at its last ordered position.
A solid-state relay failed on the servo control board of the steering gear control system and the vessel lost steering on the river.
Loss of primary steering control while departing the terminal due to a control system component failure; the crew was slow to switch to emergency steering from the bridge.
Software flaw caused a memory card failure in the water jet and engine control system of a high-speed catamaran ferry, losing steering and speed control on one hull.
A window shade chain clip touched the propulsion control touch panel and activated the station freeze function, causing temporary loss of propulsion control on a ferry.
A controllable pitch propeller blade cracked at its base from high cycle fatigue because the blade did not meet the manufacturer's design specifications.
Thread-locking fluid was not used on a feedback ring set screw, which led to failure of the controllable pitch propeller oil distribution box and loss of propulsion near the locks.
Connecting rod bolts were insufficiently torqued during the previous overhaul and the connecting rod separated from the crankshaft of a diesel generator engine.
An incorrectly sized crankshaft main bearing was installed during an engine overhaul, causing loss of lube oil pressure, generator engine failure and a fire.
Debris in the lube oil system after exceeding the recommended oil and filter change intervals destroyed an auxiliary diesel generator engine on a passenger vessel at the terminal.
Non-OEM components fitted during the last major overhaul wore prematurely; extended service intervals were inappropriate and the diesel generator failed catastrophically and caught fire.
Loosened bolts on the fuel supply inlet flange of a diesel generator sprayed fuel and started an engine room fire on a cruise ship in port; crew used the local water mist application system.
An improperly tightened pipe plug on the cylinder fuel pump housing released high-pressure marine gas oil and the fuel spray shield was attached wrongly so fuel hit the hot exhaust.
A compression fitting ferrule on fuel oil return tubing was not swaged properly, the tubing disconnected and sprayed fuel oil onto an uninsulated cylinder exhaust component.
A main engine fuel injector pump was replaced without following the manufacturer procedure, leading to a high-pressure fuel spray that ignited on exhaust components.
During bunkering, diesel oil went up the common vent line because the wrong valve type was installed in the tank fill line, and cascaded onto running machinery.
The fuel day tank without an independent vent was overpressurized because a fatigued chief engineer left the overflow valves closed, and diesel sprayed and ignited.
A hydraulic hose bent beyond its bend radius ruptured and sprayed hydraulic oil onto a hot exhaust manifold and turbocharger.
A lube oil tube on the main engine vibrated out of its joint because a retaining ring was missing, and the pressurized oil ignited on a hot exhaust surface.
Engine crew did not reinstall a plug after routine maintenance on an auxiliary generator engine; lube oil sprayed and ignited on a nearby running engine of a dredger.
A misfiring cylinder ignited lubricating oil in the engine sump and the main engine crankcase exploded.
Main engine connecting rod failure breached the crankcase and started a fire; the vessel had no fixed fire-extinguishing system and the single fire pump lost power.
Missing insulation on a generator exhaust gas pipe let radiant heat ignite combustible material nearby.
Undetected cracks in an engine muffler let hot exhaust gases escape and ignite wooden structures on the bulkhead of an accommodation space.
An O-ring seal on the composite boiler burner oil fittings block failed because the fuel ports were radially misaligned, and atomized diesel ignited on a hot surface.
A momentary abnormality in the main engine governor actuator system when responding to bridge commands caused an allision with mooring dolphins and a fire.
Control air pressure dropped because an air compressor ran at reduced output; both main engine clutches disengaged and the ferry lost propulsion during berthing.
Fuel oil leaking from a failed flange on the low-pressure fuel system of a main engine contacted a hot exhaust pipe on a ro-ro passenger ferry.
A connecting rod big end shell bearing failed and the rod penetrated the crankcase; a high oil temperature alarm before the failure should have prompted caution.
An electrical blackout occurred while the ship was moving to the berth after the electrical system was reconfigured for departure, and the vessel grounded.
A cruise ship lost propulsion in heavy weather crossing the Bay of Biscay and over 100 passengers were injured.
A large passenger cruise ship lost all main electrical power and propulsion off the Isle of Wight and its anchors fouled.
A propeller shaft sheared due to metal fatigue and seawater entered the hull through the shaft seal.
A seawater cooling supply pipe for a generator's diesel engine failed from corrosion and flooded the engine room overnight; there was no bilge alarm annunciator in the accommodation.
Thermal runaway of a lithium-ion battery bank whose battery management systems were inoperable, while charging manually with a portable charger.
A sudden block load on a generator from an electrical short starved a connecting rod of lube oil and the generator engine failed and caught fire.
A recurring but unreported steering system problem caused loss of steering control and contact with a pier; alarm labelling for critical machinery was inadequate.
Ineffective engine room resource management let the levels of the two fuel oil day tanks diverge sharply before an engine room fire on a passenger ferry.
A chief engineer was electrocuted by live 230 VAC conductors while repairing a ventilation damper circuit without using the permit-to-work system.
Leaking lube oil from a diesel generator contacted a hot engine surface and ignited; fire-damaged nonmetallic hoses on through-hull fittings then flooded and sank the vessel.
Fuel was leaking from the generator fuel supply line and ignited in the engine room; fixed-open ventilation inlets let the extinguishing agent escape.
